title: Enhancing multi-level reading comprehension through Content-Based Language Teaching: A quasi-experimental study
content:
by Yohannes Joressa Wordofa, Bedilu Teka Geleto

This study examined the effects of Content-Based Language Teaching (CBLT) on EFL students’ multi-level reading comprehension, focusing on literal, inferential, and critical dimensions. A quasi-experimental design was employed with 60 first-year university students at Mattu University, Ethiopia, divided into experimental and control groups. The experimental group received over an eight-week CBLT intervention using content-based thematic reading materials, while the control group was taught through conventional reading instruction. Data were collected using researcher-developed parallel reading comprehension tests and analyzed using MANOVA, MANCOVA, ANCOVA, and paired-samples t-tests. Results indicated no statistically significant differences between the groups at pretest, confirming baseline equivalence. However, post-intervention findings revealed a significant multivariate effect of CBLT on reading comprehension, p < .001. Follow-up analyses showed significant improvements in literal and inferential comprehension for the experimental group, while the effect on critical comprehension was not statistically significant. The findings showed statistically significant between-group differences favoring the experimental group in literal and inferential comprehension after controlling for pretest scores. However, the difference in critical comprehension was not statistically significant. The study suggests that integrating content and language instruction can strengthen reading development in EFL contexts, although higher-order comprehension development may progress more gradually. Limitations include the relatively small sample size, single-institution setting, and short intervention period, indicating the need for future longitudinal and multi-site research.
